title: What an Engram Actually Is
hook: The n-gram tables in new open models are not a trick for running 1T parameters off an SSD — they are an embedding table with a longer key, and that is a more interesting idea.
key_points: An engram is an embedding table indexed by the last 2-3 tokens (an n-gram) instead of a single token ID.
The n-gram is hashed, the stored vector is fetched, and it is fed into the model alongside the normal token embedding.
Common phrases get their own memorized vector — 'New York' is looked up as a unit, not composed from two tokens.
This moves rote factual and phrasal memorization out of the dense weights and into cheap, sparsely-accessed lookup.
It does not let you stream 980B parameters from disk: the win is a bigger memory of surface patterns, not free capacity.
content_html: When Qwen3.8-Flash-Next appeared with a large n-gram component, a story spread that engram tables would let people run trillion-parameter models with almost everything offloaded to SSD. A widely-read r/LocalLLaMA post pushed back: that is not what engrams do, and the actual mechanism is more useful than the myth.
extra_html:
The mechanism

An engram is an embedding table with a longer key. A standard embedding table maps one token ID to one vector. An engram table hashes the last two or three tokens and looks up a vector for that n-gram, which is then fed into the model alongside the ordinary token embedding. "New York" gets its own memorized vector; so does "the United". The model no longer has to reconstruct common phrases from single-token pieces every time.

Why it matters

This is a capacity trade, not a compression trick. Rote memorization of surface patterns is expensive to store in dense transformer weights, because every parameter is read for every token. A hash table is read once per position, which makes it a natural candidate for cheaper memory — system RAM rather than VRAM. That is why the tables can be offloaded while the dense weights cannot, and why the post's framing is that engrams buy a bigger phrase memory rather than free parameters. The claims here are a community explainer rather than a vendor architecture document.

flashcards.prompt: How does an engram table differ from a normal token embedding table?
flashcards.back_html: The key is longer. A normal table indexes a vector by one token ID; an engram table hashes the last 2-3 tokens and indexes a vector by that n-gram, so a phrase gets its own memorized vector.

flashcards.prompt: What is the real benefit of engram tables for local inference?

choices.text: Rote memorization moves into a cheap, sparsely-read lookup table instead of dense weights
The full parameter count can be streamed from SSD during generation
Attention becomes linear in sequence length

flashcards.explanation_html: The table is touched only for the current n-gram, so it costs little per token. What it buys is capacity for surface patterns — not a way to run arbitrarily large dense models off disk.
